concept_mcqs.explanation: The class is in package `p` and compiled under `out`, so the runtime must find `p/Hello.class` under a classpath root and the main class must be specified fully-qualified. `java -cp out p.Hello` satisfies both.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A: Omits classpath and package; the launcher searches the current dir for `Hello.class` (no package) and fails.
B: Classpath is correct but the main class name must be fully-qualified; `Hello` is not in the default package.
D: Uses a file path, but `java` expects a fully-qualified class name, not a filesystem path.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Left to right: `10+20` is `30` (numeric). `30+"30"` is string concatenation `"3030"`. Then `+40` -> `"303040"`, `+50` -> `"30304050"`. The println does not include quotes.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Treats all as concatenation from the start; but numeric addition happens until a String is seen.
C: Assumes `40+50` is added numerically at the end; but once concatenation starts, the rest are appended as strings.
D: println does not add quotes around its output.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `b += 200` is equivalent to `b = (byte)(b + 200)`. `b + 200` computes as `int` = 300, then narrows to `byte` giving 300 - 256 = 44.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Ignores narrowing back to byte.
C: A common overflow result people remember from `200` cast to byte being `-56`, but here it's `100+200` first, so 300 -> 44.
D: Simple `+=` compiles due to implicit cast; `b = b + 200` would not.

options: Compilation error due to using both `i++` and `++i` on one line.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Evaluation order is array ref, left index, then right-hand side. Left index uses `i++` (uses 1 then i becomes 2). Right side `a[++i]` increments `i` to 3 and tries to read `a[3]`, causing `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` before any println executes.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Assumes no change and that execution reaches prints; ignores the exception.
C: Assumes successful assignment and that both sides update i; fails because the RHS access throws first.
D: It compiles; Java forbids multiple modifications in one expression only when it leads to ambiguity in sequence points in some languages, not here.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Case 2 matches, there is no break, so it falls through to `default` then to `case 3` until the break. Thus `B`, `C`, `D`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Assumes `default` is skipped when a case matches; in Java it’s just a label in the fall-through chain unless guarded by breaks.
C: Assumes implicit break after each case.
D: Assumes fall-through stops before the next explicit case label, which is false in Java.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Loop iterations: start i=0 → condition uses `i++` (0%2==0) then i becomes 1, continue; loop increment makes i=2. i=2 → `i++%2==0` true, i becomes 3, continue; loop increment i=4. i=4 → true again, i becomes 5, continue; loop increment i=6, exit. `sum` never changes.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/C/D: These assume either the `continue` doesn’t skip the addition, or they mis-track the effect of the post-increment inside the `if` test in combination with the loop increment.

concept_mcqs.explanation: The enhanced for loop assigns each element value to a local copy `x`. Modifying `x` doesn’t write back to the array. The array remains unchanged.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Believes the loop writes through; it doesn’t for primitives.
C: Mixes up doubling with squaring; also still wouldn’t write back.
D: There is no iterator here; arrays don’t throw `ConcurrentModificationException` on this pattern.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `a[0]=9` mutates the caller’s array. Reassigning `b` points the local parameter to a new array; the caller’s `y` still points to the original `{2,2}`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Assumes reassignment of `b` affects the caller’s reference; Java is pass-by-value of the reference.
C/D: Assume the mutation to `a[0]` didn’t happen or that `b[0]` wrote into `y`.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `a++>1` uses 1 then a=2 → false, so `&&` short-circuits: `++b` not evaluated (b stays 1). `false || ++a>2` evaluates right side: `++a` makes a=3; `3>2` true. Final `a=3, b=1`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/C/D: Each assumes the skipped `++b` ran or that the final `++a` didn’t, misunderstanding `&&` and `||` short-circuit and left-to-right evaluation.

options: Compilation error: second dimension must be specified
concept_mcqs.explanation: `m` is a 2-length array of `int[]` with both elements initialized to null. Assigning `m[0]` leaves `m[1]` null. Dereferencing `m[1][0]` throws `NullPointerException`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Assumes a default inner array exists; it does not.
C: Index 0 would be valid if `m[1]` were an array; the failure is dereferencing null, not bounds.
D: Java allows ragged arrays with an unspecified second dimension.

scenario_questions.task: State the exact compile and run commands you would use from the project root so that the program prints `Run me`, and justify why the previous attempts failed. Your answer must explain how the package name, directory structure, and classpath interact at runtime.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
- Keep the compile step as given or re-run explicitly: `javac -d out src/com/acme/app/Main.java`. This creates `out/com/acme/app/Main.class` with the declared package name `com.acme.app`.
- Run with a classpath root that contains the `com` folder and specify the fully-qualified class name: `java -cp out com.acme.app.Main`.
- The failing commands omitted the package name. `java Main` and `java -cp out Main` both ask the launcher to find a class in the default package named `Main`. Our class is in `com.acme.app`, so the launcher looks for `out/Main.class` (or `./Main.class`) and fails. The classpath must point to the directory above `com` (here `out`), and the name passed to `java` must be the fully-qualified name that matches the package declaration.

rubric.criterion: Gives a correct compile command that produces classes under a package-matching output root (e.g., `javac -d out src/com/acme/app/Main.java`).
Gives a correct run command that includes the classpath root and fully-qualified class name (e.g., `java -cp out com.acme.app.Main`).
Explains precisely why `java Main` and `java -cp out Main` fail (mismatch between default package and declared package).
Explains the relationship between package declaration, directory structure, and classpath root at runtime.

scenario_questions.task: Propose the smallest, targeted changes to make the program print a mathematically correct average for non-empty input and handle empty input gracefully, without changing the loop structure or termination rule. Explain why your changes work with reference to Java's type and operator semantics.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
- Promote one operand to `double` during division to avoid integer division, e.g., `double avg = count == 0 ? Double.NaN : (sum / (double) count);` or `((double) sum) / count`. This changes the numeric type at the division point only.
- Guard against `count == 0` before dividing; for example, print `avg=NaN` or a clear message like `avg=undefined` when no non-negative numbers were read.
- Rationale: `sum` and `count` are `int`. In `sum / count`, integer division truncates before assignment to `double`, so `8/3` becomes `2`, then widens to `2.0`. An explicit cast to `double` on either operand triggers floating-point division. A zero-count guard prevents `ArithmeticException`.

rubric.criterion: Changes ensure floating-point division via targeted casting or promotion (no wholesale refactor).
Handles the `count == 0` case without throwing (clear behavior defined).
Explanation correctly identifies integer division and widening conversion as the root cause.
Keeps the original loop and termination semantics intact (negatives stop input).

scenario_questions.task: Identify precisely what is wrong, show the state change that causes the bad output, and provide a corrected implementation that keeps the same O(k·n) approach and also handles negative and large `k` values properly. Justify your fix succinctly.

rubric.criterion: Diagnoses the lost-element issue (failure to preserve and restore the last element).
Provides a correct in-place fix that saves last, shifts, then assigns `a[0]`.
Correctly normalizes `k` to handle negative and large values.
Demonstrates correctness on the provided example or an equivalent concrete trace.

scenario_questions.task: Rewrite the control flow minimally so the sentinel is not added to the sum, without duplicating reads or changing the sentinel value. Explain why your version avoids the off-by-one/read placement issue inherent in `do/while` here.

rubric.criterion: Provides a correct minimal control-flow fix (guarded addition or pre-checked `while`).
Avoids duplicating input reads and preserves the `-1` sentinel semantics.
Explains clearly why `do/while` as written includes the sentinel once before the check.
Shows the corrected code structure precisely (no pseudocode mistakes).

practical_tasks.title: ArrayStats: a basic CLI for numeric array statistics
practical_tasks.brief:
Build a small command-line program that computes statistics over integer inputs provided as command-line arguments. Implement the following subcommands, each as its own static method, and dispatch from `main`:
- `sum <ints...>` → print the total sum
- `avg <ints...>` → print the arithmetic mean as a decimal with exactly 2 fractional digits (round half up)
- `max <ints...>` → print the maximum
- `median <ints...>` → print the median (for even count, the mean of the two middle numbers with exactly 2 fractional digits)
Constraints: no external libraries; use arrays, loops, conditions, and your own helper methods. Do not use `Streams` or `Collections` — treat the inputs as a plain `int[]`. Package your class (e.g., `package app;`).
practical_tasks.deliverable: Source in `src/app/ArrayStats.java` (and any helper classes in `src/app/`), plus a short README with the exact `javac` and `java` commands to compile to `out/` and run each sample. No binaries.
acceptance_criteria: Compiles from project root with `javac -d out src/app/*.java` and runs from project root with `java -cp out app.ArrayStats ...`.
`java -cp out app.ArrayStats sum 5 10 -2` prints exactly `13`.
`java -cp out app.ArrayStats avg 2 3 3` prints exactly `2.67`.
`java -cp out app.ArrayStats max 9 -1 4 9 3` prints exactly `9`.
`java -cp out app.ArrayStats median 7 1 3` prints exactly `3.00`.
`java -cp out app.ArrayStats median 4 1 3 9 11` prints exactly `6.00`.
Invalid invocation (unknown subcommand or no numbers) prints a single line starting with `ERROR:` and exits without throwing.

Implementation uses at least four static helper methods: `parseInts(String[] args, int from)`, `sum(int[] a)`, `max(int[] a)`, `median(int[] a)` and a method for `avg`. Manual sort for median is implemented using loops (e.g., selection or insertion sort). No use of `Arrays.sort`.
All numeric formatting requirements (exact 2 decimals for avg/median where applicable) are met.

rubric.criterion: Correct results for sum, max, avg (with rounding), and median on provided examples.
Argument parsing and error handling: rejects bad input (non-integers, missing args, unknown subcommand) with `ERROR:` message; does not crash.
Manual array processing: median implemented via explicit in-place or copied-array sort using loops; no library sorting.
Program structure: clear method decomposition and packaged class; README shows correct `javac`/`java` commands.

practical_tasks.title: ControlKatas: three logic exercises in one CLI
practical_tasks.brief:
Implement a single packaged program exposing three subcommands that each exercise conditions, loops, arrays, and methods. Subcommands:
- `fizzbuzz <start> <end>`: For each integer from start to end inclusive, print `FizzBuzz` if divisible by 15, `Fizz` if divisible by 3, `Buzz` if divisible by 5, else the number. One line per item.
- `primecount <start> <end>`: Print the count of primes in the inclusive range. Implement `isPrime(int n)` without libraries; handle `n < 2` as non-prime.
- `collatz <n>`: Print the number of steps needed to reach 1 using the Collatz rule (n → n/2 if even, 3n+1 if odd). Use a loop; no recursion.
All outputs are plain text with no extra spaces. Use only core language features from these two modules.
practical_tasks.deliverable: Source in `src/cli/ControlKatas.java` (and optional helpers in `src/cli/`), plus a README with compile/run commands. Package the class under `cli`.
acceptance_criteria: Compiles with `javac -d out src/cli/*.java` and runs with `java -cp out cli.ControlKatas ...`.
`java -cp out cli.ControlKatas fizzbuzz 14 16` prints exactly three lines: `14`, `FizzBuzz`, `16`.
`java -cp out cli.ControlKatas primecount 1 10` prints exactly `4`.
`java -cp out cli.ControlKatas collatz 6` prints exactly `8`.
Input validation: wrong arity, non-integer args, or `start > end` for range commands prints a single line starting with `ERROR:` and does not throw.
Implementation provides separate static methods: `fizzbuzz(int start,int end)`, `isPrime(int n)`, `primeCount(int start,int end)`, and `collatzSteps(int n)`; `main` only parses/dispatches.
No external libraries or streams/collections are used; only arrays and primitives.

rubric.criterion: Correctness of fizzbuzz output (ordering, inclusivity, exact strings).
Correctness and efficiency of `isPrime`/`primeCount` for the sample (division checks up to sqrt or equivalent).
Correctness of `collatzSteps` for provided input and handling of `n <= 0` via validation error.
CLI parsing, validation, and error messaging across all commands; program does not crash on bad input.
Clear method decomposition and packaged structure; README shows correct compile/run usage.

concept_mcqs.explanation: HashSet uses hashCode to partition buckets before equals. With equals overridden but not hashCode, the two equal-looking Points likely have different hash codes (Object's identity-based), landing in different buckets; equals is never consulted across buckets, so both are kept. Size prints 2.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A: A common belief is that equals alone controls set uniqueness. In hash-based collections, equal objects must also have equal hashCode.
C: Nothing removes elements; non-sensical here.
D: All code compiles; missing hashCode is legal but incorrect for hashed collections.

options: Compilation error: C inherits conflicting defaults for f() and must override
concept_mcqs.explanation: When two interfaces provide the same default method, the implementing class must explicitly override it to resolve the conflict. Calling A.super.f() or B.super.f() is only legal from within such an overriding method; without it, compilation fails.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/C/D: Learners may think the first-declared or last-declared interface wins, or that both concatenate, but Java requires an explicit override to disambiguate.

options: Only addNums(a) compiles; addNums(b) does not
Only addNums(b) compiles; addNums(a) does not
concept_mcqs.explanation: A List<? super Integer> can be a List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object>. Both List<Integer> and List<Number> satisfy the lower-bounded wildcard and allow adding Integer values.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A/B: Confusing lower bounds with upper bounds; '? super Integer' includes Integer itself and supertypes.
D: Suggests that wildcards block all adds; lower-bounded wildcards are designed exactly to allow safe adds of the lower bound type.

concept_mcqs.explanation: The entry sits in the bucket computed with hash 1. After mutation, k.hashCode() is 2 but the map's internal bucket isn't updated. get(new K(1)) searches bucket 1, finds the mutated key that no longer equals 1, so it fails. get(k) searches bucket 2 (by the new hash) where no node exists. Both are null.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/B/D: Assume the map tracks changing hashes or that get uses identity. HashMap uses hash first, then equals within a bucket; mutating key fields breaks both retrieval paths.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Method overload resolution picks the most specific applicable method. List is a subtype of Collection, so m(List<?>) is more specific and selected at compile time. Passing null is allowed; the method body doesn't dereference it.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Belief that null matches the first-declared or least-specific overload.
C: It would be ambiguous only if neither were more specific; here List is strictly more specific.
D: Null is not dereferenced; it's only a parameter value.

options: Prints [a, c] but not reliably across JVMs
concept_mcqs.explanation: The enhanced for-loop uses an Iterator under the hood. Removing via the list directly during iteration violates the iterator's fail-fast contract and throws ConcurrentModificationException. The correct removal is via Iterator.remove() inside an explicit iterator loop or using removeIf.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A/B: Many have seen it "seem to work" in other contexts, but ArrayList's iterator is fail-fast.
D: Assumes remove is ignored; it is not, and the fail-fast triggers.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Use PECS: Producer extends, Consumer super. The source produces T values (? extends T), and the destination consumes them (? super T). With T = Integer, dst can be List<Number> and src can be List<Integer>.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
B: Constrains T to Number but still requires both lists use the same T, which nums and ints do not.
C: Overly concrete and loses generality; it would not accept List<Number> as dst unless Object is used, and it doesn't generalize.
D: Raw types compile but forfeit type safety, hiding real errors until runtime.

concept_mcqs.explanation: With accessOrder=true, iteration order is least-recently-accessed to most-recently-accessed. After accessing A it becomes most recent: B, C, A. Putting D appends it as most recent: B, C, A, D.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A: That's insertion order, not access order.
C/D: Misunderstand how access and put affect recency; only the accessed/inserted keys move to the end.

concept_mcqs.explanation: TreeSet considers two elements equal if the comparator returns 0. 2, 5, and 8 are all congruent mod 3, so only the first inserted among them (2) remains. Sorted by cmp gives [1 (mod1), 2 (mod2)].
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A: Assumes natural ordering instead of comparator behavior.
B: Assumes insertion order; TreeSet is sorted, not insertion-ordered.
D: Thinks some but not all congruent elements are kept; exactly one remains per comparator-equivalence class.

options: a1 and a3; a2 throws ClassCastException
concept_mcqs.explanation: toArray() returns Object[], which assigns to Object[] but cannot be cast to Integer[] at runtime (throws ClassCastException). The typed overload toArray(T[]) allocates an Integer[] and succeeds.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale:
A/B: Each picks one valid form but ignores the other.
D: Assumes the raw toArray returns a reifiable Integer[]; it does not.

scenario_questions.task: Explain precisely why duplicates can appear and why contains returns false in this case. Propose and show the minimal code changes to Person to make HashSet behavior correct, and discuss whether mutability of fields used in equality is acceptable here. If mutability is unavoidable, recommend an alternative design or collection choice and justify it.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies equals/hashCode contract breach as primary cause of duplicates
Explains bucket selection and why mutation after insertion breaks contains/get
Presents consistent equals and hashCode code or immutability change
Recommends viable alternative (immutable key, Map keying, or remove/re-add) with justification if mutability remains

scenario_questions.task: Propose a design that meets both requirements. Choose appropriate collections and show Java code for ordering. You must justify the choice, address generics/type-safety, and explain any trade-offs. Show how you would enqueue and dequeue tasks with your design.

rubric.criterion: Identifies instability of PriorityQueue for ties and articulates requirement clearly
Proposes correct data structure and comparator meeting both priority and stability requirements
Provides type-safe Java API and code for enqueue/dequeue without raw types
Discusses at least one alternative and its trade-offs (e.g., TreeSet or bucketed LinkedHashMap)

scenario_questions.scenario:
A library API needs a utility method that copies elements from one list to another. The naive design was:
```java
static <T> void copy(List<T> dst, List<T> src) { dst.addAll(src); }
```
but calling it with List<Number> and List<Integer> fails to compile.
scenario_questions.task: Explain why the naive signature fails. Redesign the method signature using generics and wildcards so it supports copying from List<Integer> to List<Number> (and similar hierarchies) safely. Provide a code example showing successful calls for Number<-Integer and Object<-Number. Briefly justify the variance choice.

rubric.criterion: Correctly explains invariance and why the naive <T> signature fails
Provides the correct PECS-based method signature
Demonstrates two concrete successful call sites (Number<-Integer and Object<-Number)
Justifies the variance choice succinctly

scenario_questions.task: State what method resolution will return for new Impl().tag() and why. Show how to override tag() in Impl to explicitly choose LogA's behavior (and optionally delegate to Base). Then, design a registry to map an interface Class to its handlers using collections and generics, preserving insertion order and allowing duplicates. Provide the core field and two methods: register and getHandlers(Class<?> iface).

rubric.criterion: Correctly states Java’s resolution rule (class beats interface default) and expected return value
Provides a correct override using Interface.super and/or super to control behavior
Designs a registry that preserves order and allows duplicates, with appropriate collections
Uses generics/wildcards to keep the public API type-safe

practical_tasks.title: OOP mini-application: Catalog with polymorphic pricing and behaviors
practical_tasks.brief: Build a small console application that models a product catalog with polymorphic behavior. There is a base type Item and at least three concrete subtypes (e.g., Book, Movie, Subscription). Some types implement multiple interfaces (e.g., Discountable, Downloadable). Pricing rules vary per subtype (e.g., Subscription price depends on months; Book has base price minus discount). Demonstrate polymorphism by processing a heterogeneous List<Item> and invoking behavior through base types/interfaces only. Include identity semantics: Items with the same SKU should be considered equal for catalog uniqueness. Show that a Set<Item> enforces uniqueness correctly and that lookups work reliably.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A Java project with source code and a runnable Main class that prints: 1) a polymorphic pricing summary for multiple Item instances held in a List<Item>, 2) the size of a Set<Item> before/after adding duplicates by SKU, 3) a demonstration of invoking interface-specific behavior via the interface type. Include a README with build/run instructions and the expected console output sample.
acceptance_criteria: Includes an abstract class or base class Item with at least one abstract method (e.g., price()) and shared state/behavior
Includes at least three concrete subclasses with distinct overridden behavior
Defines at least two interfaces with at least one default method; at least one class implements two interfaces; any default conflicts are resolved via an explicit override
Polymorphism demonstrated: iterate a List<Item> and call price() and a shared method without instanceof/casts
Equality contract: equals and hashCode implemented based on an immutable identifier (e.g., SKU), demonstrated with a HashSet<Item> showing de-duplication
No raw types; collections are strongly typed with generics; no unchecked warnings
Main program runs and prints the required summary, set sizes, and interface-behavior outputs matching README sample
Code compiles with a standard JDK (no external libraries required)

rubric.criterion: Class hierarchy design (base abstraction, correct overriding, coherent fields/methods)
Use of interfaces, default methods, and conflict resolution where applicable
Demonstrated polymorphism via base/interface types (no instanceof/casts for core behavior)
Correct, consistent equals and hashCode on immutable identifier; HashSet demo works
Type-safe use of generics with collections (no raw types/unchecked warnings) and runnable main/README

practical_tasks.title: Collection-based program: Generic LRU cache with eviction demo
practical_tasks.brief: Implement a generic, fixed-capacity LRU cache using LinkedHashMap in access-order mode. The cache supports get(K), put(K,V), size(), and capacity(), and evicts the least-recently-used entry on insert when full. Demonstrate that accesses update recency and that eviction is correct. Provide a small benchmark/demo in main that shows the key order and evictions.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A Java class LruCache<K,V> and a runnable Main that constructs a cache of capacity 3, performs a sequence of put/get operations, prints the cache contents (keys in order) after each step, and prints which key was evicted when eviction occurs. Include a README with the exact sequence used and the expected console output.
acceptance_criteria: LruCache<K,V> internally uses LinkedHashMap<K,V> with accessOrder=true and overrides removeEldestEntry for eviction
All public APIs are generic and type-safe; no raw types or unchecked casts
Capacity is enforced: when inserting the (capacity+1)th distinct key, exactly one eldest entry is evicted
Accessing an entry via get marks it as most-recently-used; the printed order reflects recency after each operation
Main demonstrates at least: initial fills, an access that changes order, an insertion that evicts the correct key, and a subsequent access + insertion showing updated eviction behavior
README includes build/run instructions and the expected output; Main’s actual output matches it
Code compiles and runs on a standard JDK without external libraries

rubric.criterion: Correct use of LinkedHashMap with access-order and removeEldestEntry to implement LRU semantics
Type-safe, generic public API for LruCache with clear behavior and no raw types
Accurate eviction and recency updates demonstrated by a deterministic, documented sequence
Runnable demo and README with matching expected output

concept_mcqs.explanation: In try-with-resources, if both the try block and close() throw, the primary exception is the one from the try block; the close() exception is added as a suppressed exception. Therefore the caught exception is IllegalStateException("work") with one suppressed exception from close().
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Tempting if you think the last thrown wins, but try-with-resources preserves the primary exception from the try block. C: Ignores suppressed exceptions; close() did throw, so it is recorded. D: Wrong for both which exception is primary and for ignoring suppression.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `Files.lines` returns a Stream that holds an open file/channel until the stream is closed. Wrapping each stream in try-with-resources ensures it is closed after the terminal operation.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Streams cannot be reused; also this still leaves the other files' streams unclosed. C: Materializing does not close the stream; it still needs explicit close/try-with-resources. D: Parallelism does not close resources automatically; it can make leaks worse by opening more files concurrently.

concept_mcqs.explanation: The logger is set to WARNING, so INFO is filtered out before reaching handlers. The handler initially accepts INFO and above, so W is printed. After raising the handler to SEVERE, a WARNING no longer passes, so W2 is dropped. Result: only W.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Misunderstands that the logger’s own level (WARNING) filters out INFO before the handler. C: Ignores the handler level change to SEVERE before W2. D: At least one message (W) meets both logger and handler thresholds initially.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `resolve` produces `/var/log/../data`; `normalize` removes `..` relative to the base, yielding `/var/data`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Result before normalization. C: Ignores the `..`. D: Misinterprets as relative resolution from CWD rather than absolute normalization.

concept_mcqs.explanation: The first element "A" triggers `NumberFormatException` in `map(Integer::parseInt)` before any filtering or short-circuiting applies. The exception is thrown and caught; the program prints `NumberFormatException`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/B: Assume `findFirst` short-circuits before mapping, but mapping happens first and fails on the first element. D: Wrong exception type for parsing failure.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `LocalDateTime.atZone` resolves a gap by moving forward to the next valid offset/time. 02:30 is nonexistent on that day, so it becomes 03:30 with offset -07:00.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/D: Times that would imply 02:30 or 01:30 exist in PST that day; 02:30 does not. C: `atZone` does not throw for gaps; it resolves them by shifting forward.

options:
```java
long total = Files.list(dir)
    .map(java.nio.file.Files::size) // get byte sizes
    .mapToLong(Long::longValue)
    .sum();
```

```java
long total = Files.list(dir)
    .flatMap(p -> java.nio.file.Files.lines(p)) // rely on GC to close
    .count();
```

```java
long total = Files.list(dir)
    .map(p -> java.nio.file.Files.readAllLines(p)) // OK: compiler infers throws
    .mapToLong(java.util.List::size)
    .sum();
```
concept_mcqs.explanation: Wrap the checked exception in `UncheckedIOException` and use try-with-resources around `Files.lines(p)` to ensure the stream is closed per file.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Lambdas cannot throw checked exceptions unless declared; this does not compile. C: Omits closing; relying on GC risks descriptor leaks. D: Changes the meaning (sums byte sizes, not line counts), ducking the exception rather than solving it.

concept_mcqs.explanation: Reading UTF-8 bytes as ISO-8859-1 decodes the two bytes for 'é' (0xC3 0xA9) as 'Ã' and '©', producing "cafÃ©".
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Only if both write and read used UTF-8. B: ISO-8859-1 maps all 0x00–0xFF to a character; no replacement character is used. D: Decoding as ISO-8859-1 never throws for arbitrary byte sequences.

options: It always prints the smallest multiple of 17 in the range.
It prints some multiple of 17, but which one may vary between runs.
concept_mcqs.explanation: On a parallel stream, `findAny` is allowed to return any encountered element. It will be a multiple of 17, but is not deterministic across runs.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/B: Confuse `findAny` with ordered `findFirst` or assume inherent ordering. D: There are multiples of 17 in the range, so `-1` will not occur.

concept_mcqs.explanation: I/O errors during traversal in `Files.walk` are propagated as `UncheckedIOException` from the stream pipeline. The catch prints the runtime wrapper’s simple name.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/C/D: Specific checked exceptions can be the cause, but the stream wraps them in `UncheckedIOException`. Printing the class name of the caught exception shows the wrapper, not the cause.

scenario_questions.scenario:

practical_tasks.title: Reliable File Utility

practical_tasks.title: Stream-based Data Processing with Date/Time
practical_tasks.brief: Implement a data-processing tool that reads a newline-delimited CSV file of transactions and writes two reports using streams and the java.time API.
practical_tasks.deliverable: A zip/tar containing: source code, a runnable fat JAR (or run instructions), README with usage, an input `sample-transactions.csv`, and the generated outputs `daily-summary.csv` and `top-users-weekly.csv`, plus a `processing.log`.

Output 2 `top-users-weekly.csv`: for each ISO week (system zone), list the top 3 users by total amount, columns `year-week,userId,totalAmount` sorted by `year-week` then amount desc.
Processing must be streaming: avoid loading the whole file in memory. Use `Files.lines` with try-with-resources and stream collectors.

Submission includes the exact output files generated from the provided `sample-transactions.csv` and a `processing.log` showing at least one skipped line.

rubric.criterion: Correct stream-based I/O with deterministic closure and no bulk in-memory loading
Accurate date/time handling in system zone for daily totals and ISO-week aggregation
Top-N per group implemented correctly and efficiently (e.g., comparator/collector)
Robust error handling: per-line isolation, logging of malformed lines with reason, final skipped count
Clarity of deliverables: README, run instructions, and presence of required output files/logs

options: All changes are rolled back because an exception occurred in the try block.
Only the debit is committed; the credit and audit are lost.
Both account updates are committed; the audit row is missing.
Nothing is committed because calling commit after an exception is illegal in JDBC.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Auto-commit is disabled, and no rollback occurs. The two account updates executed successfully before the audit insert failed. The catch block swallows the exception and the code calls commit after the catch, which commits whatever work is pending. The audit row is missing; balances reflect the transfer.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) Many assume exceptions auto-rollback; JDBC does not do that. You must call rollback explicitly. C) Commit is legal after catching an exception as long as the connection is open; it's how you can choose to commit partial work (even if it's a bug). D) Both debit and credit executed before the failure; there's no reason only the first update would persist.

options: JDBC swaps parameters to match column names, so amount=12.34 and account_id=42 are inserted.
A row is inserted with amount=42.00 and account_id=12 (or fails if DECIMAL→BIGINT cast is not allowed).
A SQLException is thrown before executeUpdate because setLong on parameter 1 violates the column type for amount.
Compilation fails because JDBC can detect the wrong types at compile time.
concept_mcqs.explanation: JDBC binds by index, not by column name. Parameter 1 will go into the first placeholder (amount) and parameter 2 into the second (account_id). Many databases will coerce BIGINT to DECIMAL, resulting in amount=42.00 and account_id=12. If coercion is not allowed, the driver throws at execute time, not at bind time.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) JDBC does not match by column names for PreparedStatement placeholders; it is strictly positional. C) Type checks are not compile-time; JDBC is runtime-bound. D) setLong does not fail at bind time; type issues surface when executing against the database.

options: Rows 'A' and 'C' are committed; 'B' is discarded.
Only 'C' is committed; 'A' was before the savepoint and is lost.
All three rows are committed because commit occurs at the end.
Only 'A' is committed; rolling back to the savepoint cancels the entire transaction.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Rolling back to a savepoint undoes work done after the savepoint but preserves work before it. After rollback(sp), 'B' is undone. The later insert of 'C' plus the earlier 'A' remain and commit.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) Rolling back to a savepoint does not cancel work before the savepoint. C) Commit commits the current state, which excludes 'B' due to the rollback(sp). D) Work before the savepoint ('A') is preserved, not lost.

options: executeBatch returns [-3,-3,-3,-3]; nothing persists until commit, which then also fails.
executeBatch throws SQLException with no update counts, and the transaction is implicitly rolled back.
executeBatch completes and returns [1,1,0,1]; all non-conflicting rows persist.
executeBatch throws BatchUpdateException with counts for the successful statements before the error; the first two rows persist.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Under stop-on-error, the driver applies prior statements, throws BatchUpdateException, and includes an int[] of update counts for the successful commands before the failing one. With no rollback called, those successful rows remain pending and will commit if commit is reached (here it is).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) -3 denotes Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO but is not typical here, and the driver does not return all -3 with no error. C) The batch does not continue after the failure in stop-on-error mode. D) JDBC does not implicitly roll back on error; and BatchUpdateException provides update counts.

options: The savepoint is ignored; a warning is logged but no exception is thrown.
The savepoint is created and survives across statements until connection close.
A new transaction is implicitly started for the savepoint and immediately committed.
setSavepoint throws SQLException because savepoints require an active transaction.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Savepoints are only valid within an active transaction. With auto-commit true, each statement is its own transaction; calling setSavepoint violates the contract and results in SQLException on compliant drivers.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) Savepoints cannot exist outside a transaction. C) JDBC specifies an exception for unsupported conditions; silently ignoring would be driver-specific and non-portable. D) JDBC does not implicitly start and commit a transaction for a savepoint call.

options: Replace @BeforeAll with @BeforeEach to always run it.
Make initDb static or annotate the class with @TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS).
Rename the method to setUpClass so the platform detects it.
concept_mcqs.explanation: In JUnit 5, @BeforeAll must be static unless the test instance lifecycle is PER_CLASS. Either make the method static or annotate the class accordingly.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) setUpClass is a JUnit 4 naming convention and not used by Jupiter. C) @BeforeEach runs per test but does not fix the @BeforeAll semantics issue. D) Mockito extension is unrelated to JUnit's lifecycle requirements.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Which test classes run when you execute mvn test with Maven Surefire defaults and JUnit 5?

Project has these classes:
```text
src/test/java/
  AccountSpec.java
  AccountTests.java
  ITAccount.java
  AccountIT.java
```
POM has surefire with defaults (no includes/excludes configured), and failsafe is not configured.
options: AccountTests runs; AccountIT, AccountSpec, and ITAccount are skipped.
AccountTests and AccountIT run; AccountSpec and ITAccount are skipped.
All four run because JUnit 5 detects them dynamically.
Only classes annotated with @Test run, regardless of name.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Surefire's default includes are **/Test*.java, **/*Test.java, **/*Tests.java, **/*TestCase.java. AccountTests matches; AccountIT and ITAccount are typical IT names but don't match default unit-test patterns; AccountSpec doesn't match either. Without Failsafe or custom includes, only AccountTests runs.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A) *AccountIT* does not match Surefire defaults; it's commonly run by Failsafe. C) JUnit 5 discovery still respects Surefire's file includes. D) File naming affects discovery before annotations are considered.

concept_mcqs.stem:
After rebasing your feature branch, you push with --force-with-lease. What happens to the remote?

```bash
# on branch feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# resolves fine
git push --force-with-lease origin feature
```
At the same time, a teammate may have updated origin/feature.
options: The remote is unconditionally rewritten to your history, potentially deleting teammates' commits.
The push converts your rebase into a merge on the remote to preserve both histories.
Push succeeds only if your local upstream of origin/feature is still its current tip; otherwise it is rejected to protect teammates' work.
The push always fails after any rebase because non-fast-forward updates are blocked by default.
concept_mcqs.explanation: --force-with-lease updates the remote only if the remote ref has not advanced since you last fetched. If it advanced, the push is rejected to avoid clobbering others' work.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) That's --force (without lease), which blindly overwrites. C) Non-fast-forward pushes are allowed with explicit force. D) Git does not auto-merge a rebase on push.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Two concurrent transfers deadlock occasionally. Which change most directly reduces deadlock risk?

```java
// T1
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1; // locks row 1
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2; // then row 2

// T2 (runs concurrently)
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 5 WHERE id = 2;  // locks row 2
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 5 WHERE id = 1;  // then row 1
```
Assume default isolation and row-level locks.
options: Always update accounts in ascending id order within a transaction.
Set the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE on both transactions.
Create an index on balance to make updates faster.
Use autocommit=true so each statement commits immediately.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Deadlocks arise from cyclic lock acquisition. Enforcing a consistent lock ordering (e.g., always lower id first) breaks the cycle and is the standard mitigation.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) Higher isolation can worsen lock contention and does not address the cyclic ordering problem. C) Indexing the updated column does not avoid row-lock cycles. D) Autocommit breaks transactional atomicity and can introduce other anomalies; plus it does not prevent a two-statement transfer from needing both locks.

concept_mcqs.stem:
Your POM compiles with Java 17 settings, but the build agent uses JDK 11. What happens when running mvn -q -DskipTests package?

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.11.0</version>
  <configuration>
    <release>17</release>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
```
Agent:
```text
$ java -version
openjdk version "11.0.21" 2023-10-17
```
options: Build succeeds because Maven downloads a JDK matching the release automatically.
Compilation fails: Source release 17 requires target release 17, which is unsupported by JDK 11.
Only tests fail; compilation of main sources is unaffected.
Build succeeds but the resulting bytecode runs only on Java 17.
concept_mcqs.explanation: With <release>17</release>, the compiler requires a JDK 17 toolchain. Using JDK 11 to compile for release 17 fails with an error because the toolchain cannot target a higher release than itself.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B) Maven does not auto-provision a JDK unless you configure toolchains/CI. C) It cannot produce Java 17 bytecode with a Java 11 compiler. D) The failure occurs at compilation of main sources, not only tests.

Removes/avoids committing after catching exceptions; shows correct placement of commit/rollback (and optional savepoint)

Explains caller-facing behavior and logging with useful context and safe retry semantics

scenario_questions.task: Design a test strategy and concrete changes to the code/test setup that make these tests deterministic and fast. Specify the data source choice, lifecycle annotations, and how you will reset state. Include any Maven configuration required.

Uses proper JUnit 5 lifecycle to reset state deterministically (transaction rollback or schema recreate)

scenario_questions.scenario:
Your JUnit 5 tests do not run in CI. The POM declares JUnit Jupiter, but Surefire is old. CI logs show 0 tests run. Excerpt:

```xml
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.10.1</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
<build>
  <plugins>

      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>2.12.4</version>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
```
Tests are in classes named UserRepositoryTests and OrderServiceTest.
scenario_questions.task: Diagnose why 0 tests run and specify exact POM and project changes to make JUnit 5 tests run under mvn test and in CI. Do not switch to JUnit 4.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Surefire 2.12.4 predates JUnit Platform and cannot run Jupiter tests. Upgrade Surefire to a Jupiter-capable version (2.22.0+; preferably 3.1.x). Ensure the junit-jupiter-engine is on the test classpath (the junit-jupiter BOM/pom artifact pulls it transitively in recent versions). Example fix:

```xml
<properties>
  <maven.surefire.plugin.version>3.2.5</maven.surefire.plugin.version>
</properties>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>5.10.1</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>${maven.surefire.plugin.version}</version>
      <configuration>
        <useModulePath>false</useModulePath>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>
```
Keep default test class names (they match Surefire includes). Verify with mvn -q -DskipITs test. If CI uses JDK 17+, ensure toolchain aligns with compiler settings.

rubric.criterion: Correct root cause (old Surefire cannot discover Jupiter tests)
Supplies correct plugin/dependency changes (Surefire ≥2.22.0 and Jupiter engine present)
Considers test naming/discovery and verifies mvn test in CI context/toolchain

scenario_questions.scenario:
You opened a PR from feature to main. While waiting, you rebased feature on latest main locally. After resolving conflicts, your push is rejected:

```bash
git status
# on branch feature
# your branch and 'origin/feature' have diverged

git push --force-with-lease origin feature
# ! [rejected]        feature -> feature (stale info)
```
A teammate has also pushed to origin/feature since your last fetch.
scenario_questions.task: Describe the exact, safe Git command sequence to update your remote branch so your rebased commits are pushed without deleting your teammate's work. Explain why each step is necessary and what happens to the PR.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Fetch latest refs, integrate teammate's new commits, then push with lease. Two viable approaches:

1) Rebase your local feature again on top of the new origin/feature tip:
```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/feature   # replay your rebased commits on top of teammate's
# resolve if needed
git push --force-with-lease origin feature
```
This preserves a linear history on feature that includes both sets of commits. The PR updates accordingly.

2) Alternatively, merge origin/feature into your local feature if rebasing again is undesirable:
```bash
git fetch origin
git merge --no-ff origin/feature
git push --force-with-lease origin feature
```
Explain that --force-with-lease prevents overwriting the branch if it advances again before push, and that the PR remains open and updates to show the new commit graph.

rubric.criterion: Uses fetch to update local knowledge before attempting push
Integrates teammate's commits correctly (rebase onto origin/feature or merge origin/feature)
Uses --force-with-lease (not plain --force) and explains safety
Explains PR impact (stays open; updates to new commits)
